An advertiser can wait in the pool for up to 60 days. If no agent slot opens by then, they are removed from the pool and never receive support [rules.md / Waiting pool].

The clock only matters when no slot is free. If an agent has capacity (each agent handles 10 advertisers at a time), the advertiser is assigned at once and doesn't wait at all.

In practice, I'd track two numbers: the service rate, meaning the share of eligible sign-ups in 2026 who get an agent before the wait runs out [kpis.md / Service rate], and wait time, reported as the mean and the 90th percentile for those who were assigned [kpis.md / Wait time]. If the 90th percentile creeps toward the limit, you are close to losing advertisers to removal and should look at capacity.

Firing an agent costs 40.0% of that agent's annual salary for each notice given [kpis.md / Firing cost].

The charge lands in the month the notice is given, and every notice in the plan falls in January, so the timing doesn't change the 2026 firing cost [assumptions.md / A5 Notice month]. The agent is still paid for the notice month and keeps serving the advertisers already assigned, but takes no new ones, so nobody loses support halfway through. That notice-month salary comes on top of the firing cost.

Both the salary and the firing cost are deducted from expected uplift value when we calculate net value for the year [kpis.md / Net value]. I can't give you a currency figure here because the notes don't include salary levels, but if you give me the salary for the agents you're considering, the cost is simply that salary times 40.0%.

Service rate is the share of eligible advertisers who sign up in 2026 and are assigned an agent before their 60 day wait runs out. Timing within that window doesn't matter, so someone assigned on the last allowed day still counts as served [kpis.md / Service rate].

It measures whether advertisers get served at all, not how quickly. Waiting doesn't reduce uplift unless the 60 day limit is passed. The optimizer still prefers earlier service through a small weekly penalty on uplift, because the brief asks for timely support. That choice gives up a little simulated value but cuts the average wait noticeably [assumptions.md / A9 Waiting and value].

If you need a guaranteed minimum, the service level variant of the optimizer adds a floor on the share of eligible advertisers served. Each served advertiser occupies an agent slot for the 60 day support period, so raising the floor means more headcount.

We assume the waiting pool is empty on 1 January [assumptions.md / A3 Pool on 1 January]. The brief only says agents start with no advertisers, and the history doesn't record who was still waiting on 31 December, so there was nothing reliable to carry over.

Starting empty is also the conservative choice. If the advertisers who signed up in the last 60 days of history were still waiting, the pool would open with a very large number of people. Net value would rise noticeably, and the January plan would change a lot. Remember too that anyone still unassigned after 60 days is dropped and never gets support [rules.md / Waiting pool], so a real backlog would matter quickly.
